questions.worked_solution:
First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}=\frac{A}{2x+1}+\frac{B}{(2x+1)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(2x+1)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(2x+1)^{3}$ and get

$$
4{x}^{2}=A(2x+1)^{2}+B(2x+1)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =A{(2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+1)}^{2}+B(2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+1)+C \\ 1 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)^{2} & =A(2(0)+1)^{2}+B(2(0)+1)+C \\ 0 & =A+B+1 \\ A+B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=-1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-1)^{2} & =A(2(-1)+1)^{2}+B(2(-1)+1)+C \\ 4 & =A-B+1 \\ A-B & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations $A-B=3$ and $A+B=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =3-1 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting back into $A+B=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+B & =-1 \\ B & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}=\frac{1}{2x+1}-\frac{2}{(2x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(2x+1)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2x+1}-\frac{2}{(2x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(2x+1)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x-2\int \frac{1}{(2x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(2x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+\frac{1}{2x+1}-\frac{1}{4(2x+1)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+8x+11}{(x+6)^{3}}=\frac{A}{x+6}+\frac{B}{(x+6)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x+6)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+6)^{3}$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}+8x+11=A(x+6)^{2}+B(x+6)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=-6,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6)^{2}+8(-6)+11 & =A(-6+6)^{2}+B(-6+6)+C \\ -1 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}+8(0)+11 & =A(0+6)^{2}+B(0+6)+C \\ 11 & =36A+6B-1 \\ 36A+6B & =12 \\ 6A+B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=-5$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-5)^{2}+8(-5)+11 & =A(-5+6)^{2}+B(-5+6)+C \\ -4 & =A+B-1 \\ A+B & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the equations $6A+B=2$ and $A+B=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5A & =2-(-3) \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting back into $A+B=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+B & =-3 \\ B & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+8x+11}{(x+6)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x+6}-\frac{4}{(x+6)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+6)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+8x+11}{(x+6)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x+6}-\frac{4}{(x+6)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+6)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x+6}\,\text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{(x+6)^{2}}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{(x+6)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+6|+\frac{4}{(x+6)}+\frac{1}{2(x+6)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{9-2x}{x(x-3)^{2}}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-3}+\frac{C}{(x-3)^{2}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $x(x-3)^{2}$ and get

$$
9-2x=A(x-3)^{2}+Bx(x-3)+Cx.
$$

Plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and $C$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-2(0) & =A(0-3)^{2}+B(0)(0-3)+C(0) \\ 9 & =9A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-2(3) & =A(3-3)^{2}+B(3)(3-3)+C(3) \\ 3 & =3C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=1$ and substituting the known values of $A$ and $C,$ we can solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-2(1) & =A(1-3)^{2}+B(1)(1-3)+C(1) \\ 7 & =4A-2B+C \\ 7 & =4(1)-2B+1 \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{9-2x}{x(x-3)^{2}}=\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x-3}+\frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}}
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{9-2x}{x(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x-3}+\frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|\,{|}_{1}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|\,{|}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{x-3}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)-(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-(-1+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's first factor the denominator of the integrand:

$$
\frac{5-3x}{{x}^{2}+2x+1}=\frac{5-3x}{(x+1)^{2}}
$$

We must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{5-3x}{(x+1)^{2}}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{(x+1)^{2}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+1)^{2}$ and get

$$
5-3x=A(x+1)+B.
$$

Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5-3(-1) & =A(-1+1)+B \\ B & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5-3(0) & =A(0+1)+8 \\ 5 & =A+8 \\ A & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum:

$$
\frac{5-3x}{(x+1)^{2}}=-\frac{3}{x+1}+\frac{8}{(x+1)^{2}}
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{-2}\frac{5-3x}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-3}^{-2}(-\frac{3}{x+1}+\frac{8}{(x+1)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =-3{\int }_{-3}^{-2}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x+8{\int }_{-3}^{-2}\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|\,{|}_{-3}^{-2}-8\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}\,{|}_{-3}^{-2} \\  & =-3(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-8(-1-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-8(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡2+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's first factor the denominator of the integrand:

$$
\frac{2x-1}{{x}^{2}-4x+4}=\frac{2x-1}{(x-2)^{2}}
$$

We must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{2x-1}{(x-2)^{2}}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{(x-2)^{2}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-2)^{2}$ and get

$$
2x-1=A(x-2)+B.
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2)-1 & =A(2-2)+B \\ B & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-1 & =A(0-2)+3 \\ -1 & =-2A+3 \\ A & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum:

$$
\frac{2x-1}{(x-2)^{2}}=\frac{2}{x-2}+\frac{3}{(x-2)^{2}}
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{2x-1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3}^{4}(\frac{2}{x-2}+\frac{3}{(x-2)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|\,{|}_{3}^{4}-3\cdot \frac{1}{x-2}\,{|}_{3}^{4} \\  & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)-3(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{1})-3(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
